extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democratic theory, American political reform, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of principles by which a democratic state should organize political and economic power — balancing individual liberty, social equality, and the state's constructive role in promoting distinction and public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: State authorizes discriminations: impartiality vs interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The state, whether remaining impartial or interfering, authorizes discriminations which in their effect violate the doctrine of 'equal rights.' If it remains impartial, it simply agrees to abide by the results of natural selection; if it interferes, it seeks to replace natural with artificial discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each case of state action must be considered on its merits — interference may be more costly than beneficial. The text cautions against naive appeals to a 'Square Deal' used to conceal novel purposes. Examples: interstate commerce law, pure food bill, factory legislation — all are reforms that alter market/class balances. Anti-pattern: assuming that all state interference is restorative and therefore harmless.

rubrics_metrics.name: State should exercise decisive preference in national interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A democratic state must, on the whole, make the rules in its own interest and 'help those men to win who are most capable of using their winnings for the benefit of society.' The state is likened to the bank at Monte Carlo which does not pretend to play fair but promulgates rules advantageous to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should recognize that the state cannot be a neutral umpire in economic warfare; it must set rules favoring national welfare. This legitimizes selective, purposive favoritism (constructive discrimination) rather than pretense of impartiality. Anti-pattern: pretending the state can remain completely neutral without affecting outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive discrimination: promote both individual liberty and social equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The salutary and formative democratic purpose consists in using democratic organization for the joint benefit of individual distinction and social improvement; state interference should, where possible, be exercised on behalf of both liberty and equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects the liberal view that state should act only for individual liberty (Hamilton) and argues democracies rightly pursue equality too. Policy should intentionally aim to reconcile liberty and equality in ways that advance 'human brotherhood.' Guidance includes weighing whether measures promote individual distinction while contributing to social amelioration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminations must continue to be earned and not outlast their utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages and distinctions, even when earned, should not be allowed to persist beyond their usefulness; they 'must continue to be earned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A democracy must prevent the excessive endurance of privileged positions — the state's task is to withdraw consent whenever discriminations tend to persist unduly. Anti-pattern: allowing earned advantages to ossify into permanent privilege or hereditary power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceaseless creation and replacement of elites (constructive rotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential wholeness of the community depends on the ceaseless creation of a political, economic, and social aristocracy and their equally incessant replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions and policies should encourage turnover among leaders and reward new achievement so that elites do not become entrenched. Guidance includes fostering conditions where leadership is continually tested by broad public opinion rather than insulated privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic state must represent the whole community; balance individual and social aims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the function of such a state to represent the whole community, which includes individuals as well as the mass; the state must enable individuals to exercise private purposes while maintaining social unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy should neither be devoted exclusively to liberty nor equality but should coordinate both to promote the welfare of the whole people. Anti-pattern: organizing policy solely around machinery (majority rule, suffrage) without a formative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage individual distinction by rewarding with opportunity and appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to encourage individuals to earn distinction is to reward distinction both by abundant opportunity and cordial appreciation; individual distinction, when efficient, is constructive and socially valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should create abundant opportunities and public recognition for productive achievement, not merely grant privileges. Anti-pattern: rewarding elites with privileges that remove incentives for further efficiency or social contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal suffrage generally preferable; restrict only when people incapable
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantially universal suffrage places ultimate political responsibility with those for whose benefit governments are created; limitation of the suffrage confines responsibility to a class and breeds permanent grievance. Restrictions can only be justified where the population is incapable of acting as a whole (e.g., severe social divisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor broad enfranchisement as formative for political education and unity; limited suffrage may improve short-term administrative efficiency but risks long-term instability and class antagonism. Anti-pattern: restricting franchise to minimize popular demands for economic justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of power must be conditional, accountable, and penalize abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: A democracy should delegate power to experienced, educated leaders but only on the express condition that their power is delegated and to be used, under severe penalties, for the benefit of the people as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegated authority should be time-limited, conditional, and subject to penalties for misuse to preserve ultimate popular responsibility. Anti-pattern: permitting permanent or unaccountable power to officials without mechanisms for popular resumption of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officeholders must have adequate power and independence for their duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest of individual liberty in relation to the organization of democracy demands simply that the individual officeholder should possess an amount of power and independence adequate to the efficient performance of his work (judges, executives, legislators require differing degrees of independence and term lengths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutional tenure and independence to suit functional needs: judges may need permanence for constitutional interpretation; executives need longer terms for continuity; legislators might have more restricted terms. However, permanence must be balanced by amendability of the constitutional framework so independence does not become obstructionist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate economic power as democracy does political power
rubrics_metrics.description: A democracy has as much interest in regulating for its own benefit the distribution of economic power as it has the distribution of political power; individual economic liberty should be subjected to conditions which will keep it efficient and serviceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic freedom should be preserved up to what is necessary for efficient performance, but the state should prevent concentrations of unearned or perpetual economic power that harm social bonds. Anti-pattern: treating economic liberty as sacrosanct in all forms regardless of social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent perpetuation of unearned economic distinctions (inheritance critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Very large inherited fortunes create unearned power and opportunity divorced from individual merit; the inheritor often becomes the victim of the fortune and its social consequences are corrosive to democratic solidarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should limit the social and political effects of inherited wealth (taxation, regulation, obligations) to prevent class contempt and envy and to maintain a formative relation between leaders and followers. Example: contrast creators of fortunes (earned service) with inheritors (unearned privilege).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarantee a minimum economic power/responsibility to every adult
rubrics_metrics.description: A wholesome democracy should seek to guarantee to every male adult a certain minimum of economic power and responsibility; grinding poverty and widespread partial economic deprivation are grave social dangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State policy should aim to secure a baseline standard of living to prevent economic dependence that undermines freedom and fosters political demands for redistribution. Anti-pattern: assuming political rights alone will suffice without addressing economic insecurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: State must actively raise wage-earners' standard of living to maintain loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The wage-earner is tending to make his allegiance to his union paramount to his allegiance to the state; the American state can regain the loyal adhesion of the economically less independent class only by positive service — helping them to conquer a higher standard of living without unnecessary injury to employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy should treat satisfaction of wage-earner demands as essential to public policy: improving living standards is both just and beneficial to general economic efficiency. Policy options should seek improvements that do not unnecessarily harm employers but foster broader economic productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's purpose is formative, not merely procedural
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy is not merely government by the people, majority rule, or universal suffrage; its chief advantage is their tendency to promote a salutary and formative purpose: to make expressly and intentionally for individual distinction and social improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating democratic institutions or proposals, focus on whether they further the joint ends of encouraging excellence and advancing the common good, rather than merely on procedural inclusions. Anti-pattern: evaluating democracy solely by institutional mechanics without regard to ends.
